Barrow Wood: A long mound of grey stones under the oaks, grown over with grass and bramble. Someone was laid in it long before anyone now living came to this forest, and the stones were heaped high so that they would stay. The mouth of the tomb faces the morning sun. Once its goods are taken, the cairn stands open and quiet, and it does not fill again.
Tear away the bramble and roll back the fallen stones from the tomb's mouth.
Reach into the dark chamber and bring out what was buried with the dead.

A ring of tall grey stones stands in a clearing of the wood, each leaning a little toward the one beside it, the north faces gone green with moss. On one stone, low down where the light finds it, someone cut runes long ago: Halfdan was here. The ground at the centre of the ring looks as if something was set down there and never taken up.
Walk the ring and read the runes on the low stone: Halfdan was here. Reading them calms the mind (Stress -10), once a day.
Kneel in the middle of the ring and dig through the turf with your hands.

A great grey stone as tall as a man, with a hole worn clean through it near the top, wide enough to put an arm through. Small stones have been pushed into the grass at its foot, one at a time, by people who are not here now. The oaks have leaned around it.
Look through the hole and along the line it makes toward the sunrise. The long look calms the mind (Stress -10), once a day.
Feel under the stone's foot, where people used to leave things.

A row of round stones, each the size of a loaf, set along a bank in a straight line. Every one is carved all over with spirals and knobs, and the carving is the same on each. Nothing in the forest says what they were for.
Follow the row of carved stones and trace the patterns with a finger. The slow work calms the mind (Stress -10), once a day.
Look in the grass and between the carved stones.

An ancient oak, hollow from root to crown, its trunk split open on one side wide enough to crawl through. Inside, the wood is dry and the floor is deep with old leaves. The rain does not reach it, and neither does much of the sun. It has stood like this for longer than anyone can say, and it will not fall.

Heather and thin grass over a field where a battle was fought before anyone now living came here. Bones lie in the roots, and here and there something green and pitted shows through the turf: blades and fittings gone to verdigris. Most of it was picked over long ago. What is left is a few handfuls of ground, and once those are turned the field is only a quiet field.
Work through a stretch of the field on your knees, turning the heather and sifting the earth for bone and old metal.

At the edge of the field a watchtower came down in one piece and was left where it fell: a tumble of dry-laid stone with the black ribs of its timbers sticking out. Whoever kept watch here saw the battle coming. The heap has not moved in all the years since, and what is in it can be had for the lifting.
Lever the fallen stones apart and drag out the timbers that are still sound.

A homestead at the edge of the river meadow, long since left to the weather. The roof has fallen in, the fence is down and grass grows over the threshold, but the walls still stand. Salvage what is left in the wreck first; then patch the walls and roof with planks and rope, and the place will keep the rain off again.
Work a plank or a length of rope into the broken walls and roof.
Pull the sound sticks, cord, stones and timber out of the fallen roof and the broken fence.
Lift the patched roof back onto the walls and make the homestead whole.

The old homestead, patched up and dry again. The mended roof keeps off the rain and the sun, there is room by the hearth wall to sleep, and its shelves and corners will hold about a chest's worth of your things. Left alone, the weather undoes the repairs within a month: work a plank in now and then, or it falls back into ruin and whatever it holds spills onto the floor.
Work a plank into the roof and walls to keep the weather out for another month.

A broad, worn stone by the homestead door, hollowed in the middle by years of grinding. Put rye, edible acorns or another millable thing into the hollow and work it with the hand stone to grind it into flour or powder, as a saddle quern does. It is far too heavy to carry away.
Work the hand stone back and forth over what lies in the slab's hollow.

A low grey cone no taller than a hut, its crater a pool of mud that heaves and plops and gives off a slow warmth. The ground around it is soft and warm underfoot, and the moss grows thick. Scoop from the rim and the mud wells up again.
Kneel at the rim and scoop warm mud from the crater.
The crater is spent for now; mud has not welled up again.
A white rind where the mud has dried at the edge of the springs, crusted and glittering, bitter to the tongue. Salt is hard to come by here, and the crust grows back only slowly.
Scrape the white crust into a heap with a flat stone.
The crust is scraped bare for now; it has not formed again.
Black tar wells up through the moss in a slow, warm pool, smelling of smoke and old pitch. It is thick enough to carry off in your hands while it is hot, and the pool fills again over days.
Ladle hot tar from the edge of the seep before it cools.
The seep is dry for now; tar has not welled up again.
A dark opening low under the rock overhang, its edges worn smooth. Cool, still air breathes out of it, smelling of wet stone, and a track of old footprints runs in and does not come out.
Duck under the rock and go down into the dark.
A slope of fallen stone climbs to a pale slot of daylight, the way back up to the pines.
Climb back up to the daylight.

A still black lake fills the floor of the cave, cold and clear, with a shelf of pale stone along one edge to kneel on. It never skins over and never floods, whatever the weather is doing above. In winter, when the rivers freeze and need an ice hole, it is still open water. You can drink from it, fill a container, wash in it, and fish or spear for eels and crayfish. Only a few eels live here: fish them out and the lake gives up about one a day. Like any pond's, the water is not safe to drink.
Draw unsafe lake water into the container.
Drop a line into the dark water and wait for a bite.
Stand on the stone shelf and spear what moves below.
The eels are fished out for now; give the lake a day to give up another.
Cup your hands and drink. The water is cold and not safe.
Strip off the dirt and sweat in the cold water.

A great shelf of grey rock juts out over a dry ledge, its underside black with the smoke of fires lit by people who crouched here out of the weather long ago. The ground beneath it stays dry in the heaviest rain, and the stone keeps the sun off your back. It has sheltered travellers for longer than anyone can say, and it will not fall.

The walls of this chamber are covered in paint gone the colour of dried blood and old rust. Hunters with long spears ring a herd of deer, a bear rears over a man with his arms flung up, and a line of fish swims along the foot of the wall. Handprints crowd the edges, small ones among them. Nobody has added to it in a very long time.
Hold a light close to the wall and follow the hunting scenes from one end of the chamber to the other. Studying them calms the mind (Stress -10), once a day.

Bones are heaped against the walls of this chamber in long mounds: long bones stacked like firewood, skulls set in rows along the top, the older layers sunk and gone grey. Whoever came here brought their dead down into the dark and left them. Most of what could be carried off has been, but the lower heaps have never been turned.
Kneel and sift through the lower heaps for bones still whole enough to use. Now and then something older turns up among them.

Between the Ossuary and the Sunken Lake the roof comes down to a slot in the rock, and the way on is a crawl on your belly, pushing what you carry ahead of you. Very little fits through with you: a light load of tools and food, and no more. If you carry too much, the way on is not offered, from either side, until you carry less.
Put your head and one arm into the slot and judge how much of what you carry would fit through.
A bare rock stands white in the lake, crusted thick with the droppings of the birds that nest on it, strong-smelling and good for the fields. More is laid down every day.
Scrape the dried droppings from the rock into a heap.
The rock is scraped clean for now; the birds have not laid it down again.

A shape in the cut face of the peat: a man, curled on his side, brown and creased as old leather, his skin and hair kept by the acid of the bog long after everything else about him was forgotten. A corroded green band is still clasped about one arm. He lies where the cutters found him and will not be found twice.
Ease the peat away from the body and see what he was buried with.
Steps cut into the slope with a pick and a shovel and faced with stone. While you are here the climb is easier, so a fall is less likely. Skill still counts.
A ladder lashed fast at the lip of the Fairy Hole. While you stand here the climb down is easier, so a fall is less likely. Skill still counts, and a ladder fixed at the foot helps the climb back up.

The foot of a ladder set against the shaft wall under the Fairy Hole. While you stand here the climb up is easier, so a fall is less likely. Skill still counts, and a ladder fixed at the lip helps the climb down.
You have read these stones already today; let the day turn before you read them again.
You have read this stone already today; let the day turn before you read it again.
You have traced this line already today; let the day turn before you trace it again.
You have studied these paintings already today; let the day turn before you study them again.
A lone old pine stands among the barrows, its bark split and beaded with pale resin that weeps slowly down the trunk. The scars seal over once picked, and fill again over days.
Pick the hardened beads of resin from the pine's weeping scars.
The pine has wept itself dry for now; the scars have not filled with fresh resin yet.
